lines.text: The biggest swarm ever recorded was twelve trillion bugs. Then it vanished.

parts.tts: The biggest swarm ever recorded was twelve trillion bugs. Then it vanished.
parts.heard: The biggest swarm ever recorded was 12 trillion bugs. Then, it vanished.

lines.text: 1875. Rocky Mountain locusts swept across the American West.

parts.tts: eighteen seventy-five. Rocky Mountain locusts swept across the American West.
parts.heard: 1875, Rocky Mountain locusts swept across the American West.

lines.text: One swarm was estimated at about 198,000 square miles. Bigger than California.

parts.tts: One swarm was estimated at about one hundred ninety-eight thousand square miles. Bigger than California.
parts.heard: One swarm was estimated at about 198,000 square miles—bigger than California.

lines.text: Around twelve and a half trillion insects. Guinness calls it the greatest concentration of animals ever recorded.

parts.tts: Around twelve and a half trillion insects. Guinness calls it the greatest concentration of animals ever recorded.
parts.heard: around 12.5 trillion insects. Guinness calls it the greatest concentration of animals ever recorded.

lines.text: They ate crops, wood, leather... even the clothes off people's backs.

parts.tts: even the clothes off people's backs.
parts.heard: even the clothes off people's backs.

lines.text: But less than thirty years later... they were gone.

parts.tts: But less than thirty years later...

lines.text: The last one ever collected was found in 1904.

parts.tts: The last one ever collected was found in nineteen oh-four.
parts.heard: The last one ever collected was found in 1904.

lines.text: So what wiped out trillions of locusts?

parts.tts: So what wiped out trillions of locusts?
parts.heard: So, what wiped out trillions of locusts?

lines.text: One theory: farmers. Their breeding grounds were near streams and rivers in the Rockies.

parts.tts: One theory: farmers. Their breeding grounds were near streams and rivers in the Rockies.
parts.heard: One theory, farmers. Their breeding grounds were near streams and rivers in the Rockies.

lines.note: re-voiced separately (reworded: "bred" was heard as "spread"); appended to the raw take

lines.text: Settlers plowed, irrigated and ran cattle on that exact land... and probably destroyed the eggs.

parts.heard: Settlers plowed, irrigated and ran cattle on that exact land,

lines.text: Today, their remains are still found... frozen inside a glacier in Montana.

parts.heard: Today, their remains are still found.
